reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm via combustion-gas (block) test at the coolant, coolant loss without external leak, and white smoke. Repair is replacing both head gaskets with Toyota's improved-design gaskets, resurfacing/inspecting the heads, and replacing head bolts and coolant. Check the truck's VIN with any Toyota dealer to see if SSC V06 was ever completed (it was free regardless of mileage). Use a genuine Toyota head gasket set (the superseded improved gasket, not the original part) plus new intake/exhaust gaskets and coolant. DIY parts run roughly $150-300 for a full gasket set; professional replacement is a large timing-belt-off job.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove and clean the IAC valve and throttle body bore/passages with throttle-body cleaner; inspect the connector and harness for corrosion or broken pins. Cleaning frequently restores normal idle, but a worn valve may need replacement — use an OEM/Denso IAC valve, as non-OEM units are a frequent cause of repeat P0505. Also rule out vacuum leaks, which mimic the same code. Cleaning is nearly free; an OEM IAC valve runs roughly $100-300, DIY-friendly.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove the upper and lower intake manifolds and replace BOTH knock sensors plus the knock-sensor sub-harness. Use OEM/Denso sensors only — aftermarket knock sensors very frequently fail to clear the code, forcing you to redo the whole labor-intensive job. Key parts: knock-sensor sub-harness Toyota 82219-34010; two Denso knock sensors (Denso 89615-series); new upper and lower intake manifold gaskets and a fresh coolant fill. Budget roughly $150-300 in genuine parts (harness + 2 sensors + gaskets), or ~$400-900 done at a shop given the intake teardown labor.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove the upper and lower intake manifolds and replace BOTH knock sensors plus the knock-sensor sub-harness. Use OEM/Denso sensors only — aftermarket knock sensors very frequently fail to clear the code, forcing you to redo the whole labor-intensive job. Key parts: knock-sensor sub-harness Toyota 82219-34010; two Denso knock sensors (Denso 89615-series); new upper and lower intake manifold gaskets and a fresh coolant fill. Budget roughly $150-300 in genuine parts (harness + 2 sensors + gaskets), or ~$400-900 done at a shop given the intake teardown labor.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the water pump whenever the timing belt is serviced (Toyota interval ~90k miles), and vice-versa. Do the belt, tensioner, and idler pulleys at the same time — the labor is identical. Key parts: Aisin/Toyota water pump assembly 16100-69398-83; timing belt 13568-YZZ03 (Aisin), hydraulic tensioner and idler/tensioner bearings, thermostat 90916-03075, and new coolant. Complete OEM/Aisin timing + water-pump kits are widely available (~$150-250 in parts); shop labor typically brings it to $500-900.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: First scan and inspect the wheel-speed (ABS) sensors and connectors, as dirty/damaged sensors mimic the symptoms cheaply. If the fault is the actuator/accumulator (continuous pump run, pressure faults), replace the integrated ABS actuator with master cylinder assembly - OEM 47050-60080/47050-60081 (4th gen) - and bleed/initialize the system with a capable scan tool. The part alone runs roughly $1,700-$2,300; remanufactured units are available cheaper.

Parts $120-350; DIY-friendly with an O2 socket.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose before buying a cat: scan for misfire codes (P030x/P0300), check for exhaust leaks upstream, and compare upstream vs downstream O2/A-F sensor waveforms. If sensors and exhaust are healthy and the downstream signal tracks the upstream, replace the failed converter. On 4th-gen 4.0L trucks the failure is usually the passenger-side (Bank 1) manifold-integrated cat. Use OEM or a high-quality CARB-compliant converter; a common contributing fix is the Bank 1 Sensor 2 (downstream) O2 sensor (use Denso). Sensor-only fixes run $100-300; converter replacement is the expensive path.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose before buying a cat: scan for misfire codes (P030x/P0300), check for exhaust leaks upstream, and compare upstream vs downstream O2/A-F sensor waveforms. If sensors and exhaust are healthy and the downstream signal tracks the upstream, replace the failed converter. On 4th-gen 4.0L trucks the failure is usually the passenger-side (Bank 1) manifold-integrated cat. Use OEM or a high-quality CARB-compliant converter; a common contributing fix is the Bank 1 Sensor 2 (downstream) O2 sensor (use Denso). Sensor-only fixes run $100-300; converter replacement is the expensive path.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Start cheap: verify the fuel cap seals and clicks. reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the side by noting when the noise worsens: if it gets louder turning right, the LEFT bearing is usually the culprit (and vice-versa). Check for wheel play with the tire jacked up. The standard repair on this generation is to replace the front wheel bearing/hub with an OEM or premium bearing (SKF, NSK, or Moog 'Problem Solver' are well regarded); re-torque the axle nut to spec. Because part numbers vary by exact build (2WD vs 4WD), confirm the correct hub/bearing against your VIN before ordering. Parts commonly $80-250 per side; shop labor adds $150-300 per side.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Start with a proper ATF service using the correct Toyota WS fluid and verify level/condition; old or wrong fluid alone causes harsh shifts. Scan for solenoid/pressure codes. If symptoms persist, the valve body (sticking regulator/throttle valve) or a worn shift solenoid is the likely fix - clean or rebuild the valve body or replace the affected solenoid; a transmission pressure test confirms a stuck regulator. Catching it early with fluid service can prevent a full rebuild.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: First rule out the cheap causes: check the dome/gauge fuse and inspect/scan the transmission Vehicle Speed Sensor (VSS) — a failing VSS kills the speedo signal. If fuses and VSS are good and the fault is a single stuck/erratic needle, the cluster's stepper motor(s) are the cause. Repair by replacing the failed stepper motor(s) (common X27.168-type) or sending the cluster to a rebuild service; full cluster replacement requires mileage transfer to stay legal. Stepper-motor DIY repair is inexpensive ($10-40 in motors); professional cluster repair/replace runs $150-350.

Repair by replacing the failed stepper motor(s) (common X27.168-type) or sending the cluster to a rebuild service; full cluster replacement requires mileage transfer to stay legal. Stepper-motor DIY repair is inexpensive ($10-40 in motors); professional cluster repair/replace runs $150-350.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: For whine, first siphon the reservoir, clean the internal filter screen with brake cleaner, and refill with fresh Dexron II/III ATF — this alone often cures the noise. For leaks, pinpoint the source: replace the union-bolt sealing washers/gaskets for pump-fitting leaks, replace worn high-pressure/return hoses, or reseal/replace the pump if the shaft seal is leaking. Always refill with ATF, never generic PS fluid. Cleaning/flush is nearly free; hoses/gaskets $30-120; a replacement pump runs $120-350 in parts.

Always refill with ATF, never generic PS fluid. Cleaning/flush is nearly free; hoses/gaskets $30-120; a replacement pump runs $120-350 in parts.

For leaks, pinpoint the source: replace the union-bolt sealing washers/gaskets for pump-fitting leaks, replace worn high-pressure/return hoses, or reseal/replace the pump if the shaft seal is leaking. Always refill with ATF, never generic PS fluid. Cleaning/flush is nearly free; hoses/gaskets $30-120; a replacement pump runs $120-350 in parts.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: First swap the rear-window relay in the engine-bay fuse box with an identical relay to rule it out, and try the regulator reset (hold the switch 2+ seconds past full-open and again past full-close). If the glass still won't operate, replace the rear back-door power window regulator/motor sub-assembly: OEM 69807-35030 (2010-2024) or 69807-35020 (2003-2009). Replacement takes 1-2 hours and requires removing the tailgate trim.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect the rest of the cooling system before condemning the pump. Check reservoir level, pulley/bearing play and smoothness, and press a dry paper towel against cleaned pump-area residue. Dry residue alone does not require replacement; wet coolant, an active drip, excessive bearing play, or rough rotation does. If replacement is confirmed, use the model-year repair procedure and verify the pump and separately sold gasket by VIN. Toyota lists exact pump assembly 16100-09515, but the part page itself requires a vehicle-fitment check. Do not automatically replace the belt, tensioner, thermostat, or coolant as separate failures without inspecting them.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the fault is the converter and not the downstream oxygen sensor or an exhaust leak: inspect for exhaust leaks at the manifold/flex pipe, and check rear O2 sensor switching before condemning the cat. OEM Toyota bank-1 converters are pricey ($500-1200); CARB-compliant aftermarket direct-fit units (Walker/Magnaflow/Eastern) run $150-400. Replace the downstream O2 sensor if aged.

Check whether the specific paint code fell under any Toyota goodwill/warranty extension.

Clear codes and verify start/idle after repair.

Torque the axle nut to spec and confirm the clicking is gone on test drive.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove the EGR valve and modulator/tube and clean the carbon from the valve, ports and the small EGR passage in the intake manifold (a stuck pintle can be freed). Test the EGR VSV (vacuum switching valve) for correct operation and replace if it does not hold/switch vacuum. Reset the ECM after cleaning. OEM parts: EGR valve 25620-15070/25620-74240-type depending on engine, EGR VSV 25860-xxxxx (confirm exact PN by VIN); aftermarket Standard/Beck-Arnley cross-references are available. Verify the exact PN against the vehicle since 1.6L 4A-FE, 7A-FE and early 1ZZ-FE use different valves.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove the EGR valve and modulator/tube and clean the carbon from the valve, ports and the small EGR passage in the intake manifold (a stuck pintle can be freed). Test the EGR VSV (vacuum switching valve) for correct operation and replace if it does not hold/switch vacuum. Reset the ECM after cleaning. OEM parts: EGR valve 25620-15070/25620-74240-type depending on engine, EGR VSV 25860-xxxxx (confirm exact PN by VIN); aftermarket Standard/Beck-Arnley cross-references are available. Verify the exact PN against the vehicle since 1.6L 4A-FE, 7A-FE and early 1ZZ-FE use different valves.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Maintain strict oil-change intervals with correct-viscosity oil (low oil level/pressure worsens the rattle). reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Check engine oil level/condition first (VVT faults often stem from low or degraded oil). Remove the camshaft timing oil control valve, clean the OCV and its filter screen; if the plunger is sticky or the solenoid fails a resistance/actuation test, replace it. OEM PN 15330-22030 (fits 2000-2008 Corolla 1ZZ-FE; also Celica/Matrix/MR2), roughly $50-90; Denso/Standard aftermarket cross-references available. Clear codes and verify cam timing response after replacement.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the water pump with the revised OEM design (Toyota assembly 16100-39466, which supersedes 16100-39465 and includes pulley and gasket) or a quality Aisin WPT-140 unit; verified aftermarket cross-refs include OAW T7480 and Aisin WPT-140. Replace the gasket and refill with Toyota SLLC (pink) coolant, then bleed the cooling system. Inspect the serpentine belt while access is open. Catch early signs (pink residue near the front-center/passenger side of the block or a faint whine) before overheating occurs. Typical mileage to first failure ranges widely; many owners do it preventively around 90,000-120,000 miles.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the consumption rate with a documented oil-consumption test (dealers historically used a ~1 qt/1,200 mi threshold). Remedies range from shortening oil changes to ~5,000 miles, to a piston-soak/ring-decarbon procedure, up to replacing the piston rings (and sometimes pistons) if rings are carbon-locked. Use the correct 0W-20 spec. A ring/piston job is labor-intensive (commonly $1,500-$3,500); decarbon/soak and a maintenance-interval change are the cheaper first steps. Check the dash/oil light frequently to avoid running it dry.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose with a leak/dye test and pressure check. Replace the condenser (sealant/weld repairs rarely hold and can contaminate the system), then evacuate and recharge with the correct refrigerant and oil charge. The condenser itself is usually ~$100-$250; full replacement with evacuate/recharge commonly runs $600-$1,100 at a dealer (roughly a 2-hour job plus refrigerant). A protective grille/condenser screen can reduce repeat rock damage.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose before replacing: verify no exhaust leaks, check for oil/coolant consumption that poisons the cat, and scope O2/AF sensor switching. Clear codes and re-run readiness monitors.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: For wind noise, have the A-pillar/windshield weatherstrip and mirror seals inspected and the applicable TSB seal correction applied; owner-level fixes include adding window/foam insulation under the hood weatherstrip and reseating the A-pillar trim. For the sunroof rattle, applying 3M clear silicone paste to the moonroof rail channel and the black glass actuators is a common, effective owner fix; a dealer may reseat or shim the glass. Costs are usually low ($0-$200) and largely labor/diagnostic; under warranty the seal TSB should be free.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the integrated brake actuator assembly and re-initialize/program it with Toyota Techstream (the new unit must be calibrated and bled). For the 2006-2007 Highlander Hybrid the actuator is Toyota PN 44050-48191; 2008-2013 use 44050-48320 — verify by VIN. This is expensive: the part alone runs ~$1,200-$1,800 and full dealer replacement quotes range from roughly $2,600 to $3,500+. Independent hybrid specialists can be cheaper.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the inverter cooling electric water pump and refill/bleed the inverter coolant loop (air-bleed procedure is required). For the 2006-2010 Highlander Hybrid the drive-motor inverter cooler water pump is Toyota PN G9040-48080 (non-tow); tow-package and later years use a different pump (e.g., G9020-48xxx family) so verify by VIN/configuration. reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the liftgate struts/gas props and the power lift arm actuator inspected; replace failed gas struts in pairs and replace the power lift arm/actuator if it has separated or the hinge is bowed. Many owners with minor faults restore function by cleaning the latch/tracks, realigning or replacing the latch, and resetting the system (disconnect/reconnect the battery, then re-initialize the open/close memory). Strut replacement is inexpensive (roughly $80-$250); a full power lift arm/actuator and hinge repair at a dealer can run well over $1,000.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Find the entry point with a controlled water test. Reseal or replace the taillight gaskets (a frequent culprit), replace the hatch/liftgate weatherstrip if cracked, reseal the third brake light and the rear spoiler/air-deflector bracket foam, and clear clogged drains. Dry the spare-tire well and treat any surface rust. Most fixes are inexpensive seals and labor ($50-$300); ignoring it risks far costlier corrosion and electrical/backup-camera damage.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the source with a cold-start listen and a smoke/soap test at the manifold-to-head flange and along the manifold casting (a cracked manifold gets louder under light load/acceleration, unlike the harmless injector tick). Replace the cracked manifold(s) with OEM or quality aftermarket units and new manifold gaskets and hardware; many shops replace both banks while access is open. Use new exhaust manifold-to-head nuts/studs and the OEM gasket to prevent a repeat leak. Replacing only the gasket will not cure an actual casting crack.

Replace head bolts per spec if torque-to-yield. Verify no oil-in-coolant or coolant-in-oil contamination that would indicate further damage.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the dealer perform a parasitic-draw test (target draw is a few tens of mA after modules sleep) and check for any software/firmware update for the DCM/telematics and body modules that reduces standby current. Inspect and tighten the 12V battery terminals (loose negative terminals are a documented false cause of charging warnings), load-test/replace a weak factory 12V battery, and verify charging-system output. For trucks parked for extended periods, a battery maintainer or disconnect prevents repeat dead-battery events while a permanent fix is pending. Most affected trucks are within the new-vehicle warranty.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the dealer perform a parasitic-draw test (target draw is a few tens of mA after modules sleep) and check for any software/firmware update for the DCM/telematics and body modules that reduces standby current. Inspect and tighten the 12V battery terminals (loose negative terminals are a documented false cause of charging warnings), load-test/replace a weak factory 12V battery, and verify charging-system output. For trucks parked for extended periods, a battery maintainer or disconnect prevents repeat dead-battery events while a permanent fix is pending. Most affected trucks are within the new-vehicle warranty.
